pos: n. (Jan Seklucjan, c. 1510–1578, publisher of the first printed Polish New Testament)
etymology: Polish Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Seklucjan, of Sieklucz, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Jan Seklucjan was driven out of Poznan for preaching the gospel and found refuge at Konigsberg under Duke Albrecht of Prussia, who gave him a pulpit and a press. From there he supplied Poland with what Poland did not yet have: a Polish catechism, a Polish hymnbook, and between 1551 and 1553 the first printed Polish New Testament, translated by the young scholar Stanislaw Murzynowski and seen through the press by Seklucjan himself. He was not the translator and he said so. He was the man who decided the thing should exist, found the scholar, raised the money, argued with the censors and sold the copies. The dictionary gives him the entry on that ground. Every vernacular Scripture in Europe required two gifts, and they are seldom in the same man: somebody who can render the Greek, and somebody who will not rest until the rendering is printed and in a cart going south. Seklucjan was the second kind, and the Polish Reformation began with his cartloads.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines publish as to send a book into the world, and patron as one who countenances and supports.
webster_full: PUB'LISH, v.t. To send a book into the world; to make known to mankind or to people in general.
PA'TRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a defender.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers.
TESTAMENT, n. The name of each general division of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures.
scriptures: The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
corruption_summary: Exiled from Poznan, he found a translator and a press and gave Poland its first printed New Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of crediting a translation to its scholar alone, which quietly teaches that the gospel travels by learning. Learning is necessary and it is not sufficient. Murzynowski construed the Greek; Seklucjan got the book into Poland, and without the second labour the first would have stayed in a drawer at Konigsberg.

The principle to recover is that the publishing is itself the Lord's work and is named as such. “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11) — a company, not a scholar. The written word is to be made plain and portable: “make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). And Paul's chain of necessity ends where Seklucjan worked — “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).

pos: n. (Mikolaj Rej, 1505–1569, Polish layman, Calvinist, the first great writer of Polish prose and verse)
etymology: Polish Mikolaj from Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; Rej, a Polish surname of disputed origin.
biblical_def: Mikolaj Rej was a country gentleman with no university degree who decided that Polish was fit for serious writing and proved it. He is the father of Polish literature by common consent, and he was a convinced Calvinist who put his pen at the service of the Reformed cause: a Polish Postylla of sermon expositions covering the church year, a paraphrase of the Psalms, a long satirical poem on the estates of the realm, and the Zwierciadlo, a mirror of the godly life of a Polish nobleman. The dictionary names him as the type of the lay teacher. Rej was not ordained and never pretended to be; he wrote so that a gentleman and his household, reading aloud in the evening on an estate days from the nearest Reformed pulpit, would have sound exposition in their own tongue. The Polish Reformation ran largely through the nobility's households, and the book that most often reached those households was written by one of their own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines laity as the people as distinguished from the clergy, and mirror as that which gives a true representation.
webster_full: LA'ITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.
MIR'ROR, n. A looking glass; any thing which gives a true representation or in which a true image is seen.
POS'TIL, n. A short comment or explanatory note on a text of Scripture.
PAR'APHRASE, n. An explanation of some text in a more clear and ample manner than the words of the author.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: An unordained country gentleman who wrote Polish postils for the households of the Polish nobility.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the clericalising of teaching, which lets a Christian father conclude that instruction is somebody else's office and his own house a congregation without a pastor. Rej's readers were often three days' ride from a preacher. His books assumed that the head of a household would read aloud and expound, because nobody else was going to.

The principle to recover is that household instruction is commanded of fathers and not delegated. The word is to be taught at home and on the road: “And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deu 11:19). The generations are to be told on purpose: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). And the resolution is made by a man for his own house — “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15).

pos: n. (Grzegorz Orszak, c. 1520–1567, rector of the Pinczow school and a translator of the Brest Bible)
etymology: Polish Grzegorz from Greek Gregorios, watchful; Orszak, a Polish surname, a retinue or train.
biblical_def: Grzegorz Orszak ran the school at Pinczow, which under the patronage of the Olesnicki family became the intellectual centre of the Polish Reformed church — a gymnasium on the Strasbourg model that trained a generation of Polish ministers and gentry. From that base he worked on the Polish version of the Scriptures commissioned by Prince Mikolaj Radziwill and published at Brest in 1563, the first complete Polish Bible made from the original tongues. He also wrote a Polish catechism and a confession. The dictionary records him for the pairing of school and Bible, which is not accidental. A vernacular Bible needs men who can read Hebrew and Greek, and such men are produced by schools; a school needs a text to teach, and the Brest Bible gave Polish ministers one. Orszak's later years were troubled by the antitrinitarian controversy that tore the Polish church, and the Pinczow circle itself divided over it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gymnasium as a place of exercise and a school for the higher branches, and original as the tongue in which a book was first written.
webster_full: GYMNA'SIUM, n. In Germany, a school of the higher order, intermediate between a common school and a university.
ORIG'INAL, a. First in order; preceding all others; as the original languages of Scripture.
REC'TOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; the master of a school.
CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised and which members of a church subscribe.
scriptures: Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: He ran the Pinczow school and helped translate the Brest Bible of 1563 from the original tongues.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the pitting of piety against learning, which flatters the lazy on both sides: the scholar who does not pray and the preacher who will not construe. The Polish Reformation's one complete Bible from Hebrew and Greek came out of a school, and when the school divided the Bible work stopped.

The principle to recover is that God gives learning as a gift and uses it, while refusing to let it stand in the place of faith. “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17) — the gift is named as His. Wisdom is to be deliberately sought: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Pro 4:7). And the end of the whole labour is the end Paul gives Timothy — scriptures “which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 3:15).

pos: n. (Mikolaj Radziwill the Black, 1515–1565, Lithuanian magnate and patron of the Brest Bible)
etymology: Polish Mikolaj from Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; Radziwill, a Lithuanian princely surname.
biblical_def: Mikolaj Radziwill the Black was Grand Chancellor of Lithuania and the richest man in the Grand Duchy, and he spent a great deal of that wealth on the Reformed church. He turned churches on his estates over to Reformed ministers, founded a press at Brest, paid the scholars who produced the complete Polish Bible of 1563 that bears his patronage, and corresponded with Calvin, who dedicated his commentary on Acts to him. Within two generations his line had returned to Rome and his grandchildren were endowing Jesuit colleges, and the Lithuanian Reformed church shrank with its patrons. The dictionary records both halves. Radziwill's money bought the Brest Bible, which outlasted his house's religion; the Polish-Lithuanian Reformation's weakness was precisely that it was carried by magnates rather than by congregations, so that a change of heart in one family emptied a county's churches. Patronage is a gift and a danger, and this is the clearest European case of both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines magnate as a person of rank or distinction, and patronage as the support or protection afforded by a patron.
webster_full: MAG'NATE, n. A person of rank; a noble or grandee.
PA'TRONAGE, n. Special countenance or support; favour or protection extended to a person or cause.
CHAN'CELLOR, n. A high officer of state, presiding over a court or a chancery.
ENDOW', v.t. To furnish with a permanent fund of property for support.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Jer 2:21
Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?
Luk 8:13
They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.
corruption_summary: His wealth bought the Brest Bible of 1563; his grandchildren endowed Jesuit colleges instead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a strategy rather than a doctrine: the conviction that the way to reform a nation is to convert its powerful, after which the people will follow. Poland and Lithuania ran that experiment at full scale. The magnates were converted, the churches were given over, the Bible was printed — and when the magnates' grandsons changed their minds the congregations had no root of their own and went with them.

The principle to recover is that the arm of flesh cannot hold a church, however generous it is. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). The king's heart is in God's hand and not in the church's — “he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). And the warning about rootless profession is exact: those of whom it is said that “these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away” (Luk 8:13).

pos: n. (Szymon Zacjusz, c. 1507–1591, first superintendent of the Reformed church in Lithuania)
etymology: Polish Szymon from Hebrew Shimon, hearing; Zacjusz, a latinised Polish surname.
biblical_def: Szymon Zacjusz was the first superintendent of the Reformed churches of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, appointed under Radziwill's protection at Vilnius. He organised a scattered set of congregations into a church with synods, ordained ministers, discipline and a catechism, and he spent the latter part of his ministry resisting the antitrinitarians who were making rapid progress among the Lithuanian gentry. He wrote against them, pressed for subscription to the Trinitarian confession, and was pushed out of Vilnius for his pains before being restored. The dictionary names him for the unglamorous labour of constitution-making. Lithuania had Reformed preaching before it had a Reformed church; what Zacjusz supplied was the structure — who ordains, who may be deposed, what must be believed to hold a pulpit — without which preaching produces a movement and not a church, and a movement cannot be defended against heresy because it has no boundary to defend.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines synod as an ecclesiastical council, and discipline as the correction and government of a church.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council; a meeting of ministers and elders to consult on matters of religion.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors; the government of a church.
SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of some place, person or business.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation given by underwriting the name.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Whosoever transgresseth, and abideth not in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God. He that abideth in the doctrine of Christ, he hath both the Father and the Son.
corruption_summary: He gave the Lithuanian Reformed churches synods, discipline and a Trinitarian subscription to hold a pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is the antitrinitarianism that swept the Lithuanian and Polish gentry in the 1560s and hardened into the Minor Church, denying that the Son is God of God. Zacjusz met it not only with argument but with a requirement: that a man subscribe the faith before he is given a pulpit. The modern instinct is to hear that as institutional coldness. It is in fact the only mechanism by which a church protects the people in the pews from a plausible man.

The principle to recover is that church order is appointed by God and is a means of preserving doctrine. Titus was left in Crete “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). The Jerusalem council did not merely debate; it issued a judgment: “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28). And the boundary is stated by John without apology — “Whosoever transgresseth, and abideth not in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God” (2Jo 1:9).

pos: n. (Krzysztof Trecy, c. 1530–1591, Polish Reformed minister at Krakow and correspondent of the Swiss churches)
etymology: Polish Krzysztof from Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; Trecy, latinised as Trecius.
biblical_def: Krzysztof Trecy studied in Switzerland, knew Bullinger and Beza personally, and came back to spend thirty years as the minister of the Reformed congregation at Krakow and the secretary of its synods. His letters to Zurich and Geneva are the fullest surviving account of what happened to the Polish Reformed church in those decades, and what they mostly describe is the antitrinitarian secession and the long effort to hold the remaining churches to the Trinitarian faith. He translated, he taught in the Krakow school, and he laboured for the Consensus of Sandomierz of 1570, by which the Reformed, the Lutherans and the Bohemian Brethren in Poland agreed to recognise one another's ministries and sacraments against the common Roman and antitrinitarian pressure. The dictionary values that Consensus. It was a limited agreement between churches that still differed on the Supper, made because they agreed on the Godhead of Christ, and it is a model of what unity can honestly be when it is built on doctrine rather than on silence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines consensus as agreement, and secession as the act of withdrawing from fellowship or communion.
webster_full: CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; concord; accord.
SECES'SION, n. The act of withdrawing, particularly from fellowship and communion.
COM'ITY, n. Courtesy; civility; mutual regard between bodies or churches.
CORRESPOND'ENCE, n. Intercourse between persons at a distance by means of letters.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
I and my Father are one.
corruption_summary: He laboured for the Sandomierz Consensus of 1570, a union built on the Godhead of Christ rather than on silence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern ecumenical method, which secures agreement by declining to state what the parties believe and calls the result unity. Sandomierz did the opposite: the Reformed and the Lutherans wrote down what each held on the Supper, declined to pretend they agreed, and then recognised one another on the ground of the Trinitarian and gospel faith they did hold in common against the Socinians.

The principle to recover is that fellowship follows agreement and cannot be manufactured without it. “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3). Paul asks for sameness of speech, which presumes a stated content: “that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10). The bond is to be kept by effort, not by vagueness — “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — and the article the Polish churches would not surrender for any union is the Lord's own: “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30).

pos: n. (Stanislaw Sarnicki, 1532–1597, Polish Reformed superintendent and opponent of the antitrinitarians)
etymology: Polish Stanislaw, he who stands in glory; Sarnicki, of Sarnik, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Stanislaw Sarnicki studied at Wittenberg, came home a Reformed minister, and became the chief organiser of the Polish Reformed churches in their hardest decade. When the antitrinitarians separated in 1563 and formed the Minor Church, Sarnicki led the Major Church that remained, presided over its synods, pressed the Trinitarian subscription, and wrote both the polemic against the seceders and the first collection of Polish Reformed church orders. He was also a historian and a geographer of some seriousness, and he published annals of the Polish kings. The dictionary names him as the man who kept a church in existence during a schism. That work is not attractive: it consists of synods, subscriptions, deposed ministers, disputed buildings and bitter pamphlets, and nobody writes hymns about it. But the Polish Reformed church that survived into the seventeenth century, printed the Gdansk Bible and sent students to Heidelberg, survived because Sarnicki and men like him would do that work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schism as a division in a church, and annals as a history digested in the order of time.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. A division or separation in a church or denomination, occasioned by diversity of opinions.
AN'NALS, n. A history digested in the order of time; a relation of events in chronological order.
POLEM'IC, a. Controversial; disputative; as a polemic treatise or divine.
OR'DER, n. Established mode of proceeding; rule; regularity; the ecclesiastical constitution of a church.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine,
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: He led the Polish Reformed church through the antitrinitarian schism of 1563 and wrote its church orders.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is Socinianism in its Polish cradle. The Minor Church that separated in 1563, with Giorgio Biandrata and later Faustus Socinus among its guides, denied the eternal Godhead of the Son and in time the satisfaction He made, and it produced in the Racovian Catechism the most influential denial of the Trinity written in early modern Europe. Sarnicki's pamphlets against it are rough reading, and the dictionary does not apologise for their roughness: the men he was answering were taking congregations with them.

The principle to recover is that contending for the faith is commanded, and that it is a pastoral act rather than a failure of charity. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). Paul predicted exactly this shape of trouble: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). The charge given to Timothy at Ephesus was to stop it — “that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine” (1Ti 1:3) — and the elder's qualification includes the ability to do it: “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

pos: n. (Andrzej Wolan, c. 1530–1610, Lithuanian Reformed nobleman, diplomat and writer on political liberty)
etymology: Polish Andrzej from Greek Andreas, manly; Wolan, a Lithuanian-Polish surname.
biblical_def: Andrzej Wolan was a Lithuanian gentleman in the service of the Radziwills and then of the crown, a diplomat, and a lay elder of the Reformed church who wrote on both divinity and politics. His best-known book argues for political liberty under law as the proper condition of a Christian commonwealth, and he defended the Reformed faith against both Rome and the antitrinitarians in print. He belonged to the generation that had the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, by which the Polish-Lithuanian nobility bound themselves to keep religious peace among themselves — an arrangement unique in Europe at the time, and one which the Counter-Reformation afterward dismantled by patience rather than by force. The dictionary records Wolan as a Christian layman thinking about the state, and distinguishes his argument from its modern imitation. He did not hold that truth is private or that the magistrate has no interest in religion; he held that a conscience cannot be coerced into faith and that a commonwealth of free men is governed by law rather than by will.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint, and commonwealth as the whole body of people in a state.
webster_full: LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without any restraint but that of law.
COM'MONWEALTH, n. An established form of government; the whole body of people in a state; a republic.
CON'SCIENCE, n. The faculty or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions and affections.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
scriptures: Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: A lay elder and diplomat who argued for liberty under law as the condition of a Christian commonwealth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reading of sixteenth-century toleration arguments as early liberalism, as though men like Wolan had held that religious truth is a private preference. They held nothing of the kind. Their argument was that faith is produced by the word and the Spirit and cannot be produced by a sword, from which it follows that compelling a man's profession makes a hypocrite rather than a believer.

The principle to recover is that Christian liberty is freedom from sin and from men's inventions in worship, and that it is not licence. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1). Peter closes the gap before anyone can walk through it: “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God” (1Pe 2:16). And the magistrate remains God's servant and not the church's rival — “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).

“Righteousness exalteth a nation” (Pro 14:34) — the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 and its slow unmaking.

pos: n. (Krzysztof Krainski, 1556–1618, Polish Reformed superintendent, author of the Postylla and the Agenda)
etymology: Polish Krzysztof from Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; Krainski, of Kraina, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Krzysztof Krainski was superintendent of the Reformed churches of Lesser Poland in the generation when the Counter-Reformation was closing in, and his two great books were written for churches that were losing ground. The Postylla supplied Polish expositions for the whole church year; the Agenda supplied the forms — how to baptise, how to administer the Supper, how to marry, how to bury, how to visit the sick and comfort the dying — so that a minister in an isolated congregation, or in the end a layman where no minister could come, had the order of the church in his hands. He also wrote a history of the Polish Reformed church. The dictionary names the Agenda as the more important of the two. A church under pressure loses its ministers first and its buildings second; what it can keep is a known form of sound words, and Krainski was writing to make sure that when the pastor was gone the people would still know how the church of Christ does things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agenda as a memorandum book of things to be done, and form as a model, a prescribed order of words.
webster_full: AGEN'DA, n. A memorandum-book; among divines, the things to be done, as distinguished from matters of belief.
FORM, n. A model; a draught; a pattern; a prescribed order of words, as a form of prayer.
POS'TIL, n. A short comment or explanatory note on a text of Scripture.
AGEN'DUM, n. A thing to be done; a service to be performed.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: His Agenda put the church's forms into the people's hands against the day the minister was taken away.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a contempt for forms as such, as though a settled order of words were the enemy of sincerity. Krainski was writing for congregations that would shortly have no minister, and his forms were the means by which an orphaned church could still baptise its children and bury its dead as Christians rather than inventing something.

The principle to recover is that sound words are given a pattern and the pattern is to be held. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). Paul commends a church for keeping delivered order: “keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you” (1Co 11:2). And the old path is to be asked for and walked in rather than improvised — “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).

“keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you” (1Co 11:2) — baptism, Supper, marriage and burial set down.

pos: n. (Daniel Mikolajewski, c. 1560–1633, chief reviser of the Gdansk Bible of 1632)
etymology: Hebrew Daniyyel, God is my judge; Mikolajewski, son of Mikolaj, a patronymic surname.
biblical_def: Daniel Mikolajewski was a minister of the Bohemian Brethren's Polish branch who spent the last stretch of his life revising the Polish Scriptures. The Brest Bible of 1563 had become scarce and was criticised for leaning on the Latin and French; the antitrinitarians had produced their own version; and the Polish Protestant churches, now a shrinking minority, needed one text they could all use. Working chiefly with Jan Turnowski, Mikolajewski produced the revision printed at Gdansk in 1632, which from that day until the twentieth century was simply the Polish Protestant Bible, as the Authorized Version was the English one. The dictionary places him at the close of this batch for that reason. The Polish Reformation lost its magnates, its schools, most of its churches and in the end its legal standing, and what came through the loss was a book. A church may be reduced to a remnant and still hand on an unabridged Bible, and the remnant that does so has handed on everything necessary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revise as to review and correct, and remnant as that which is left, a residue.
webster_full: REVI'SE, v.t. To review; to re-examine; to look over with care for correction.
REM'NANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
RECEN'SION, n. Review; examination; enumeration; a revised text.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
scriptures: Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: He produced the Gdansk Bible of 1632, the Polish Protestant Bible for the next three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of a church's health by its visible strength, which would have written off Polish Protestantism in 1632 and been wrong. The congregations were few and getting fewer. The Bible they printed in that year was read by Polish-speaking Protestants in three empires for three hundred years.

The principle to recover is that God preserves a remnant and preserves His word, and that the second is how the first survives. “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9). Paul applies it to his own day: “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). The text itself is not to be added to or cut down — “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2) — and it outlasts everything that printed it: “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

roots_lines: Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, one left remaining; Isaiah 1:9.
Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant, a remainder; Romans 11:5.
Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase; Deuteronomy 4:2.
Hebrew gara (H1639) — to diminish, to take away; Deuteronomy 4:2.

“neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2) — a revision made against the antitrinitarian version.
“but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — the Gdansk Bible read for three centuries.
